paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A divergent boundary is a linear feature lying between two tectonic plates as they move apart. Other names for it are constructive boundary and extensional boundary. Most active divergent boundaries lie between oceanic plates and take the form of mid-oceanic ridges. Inside continents, they at first produce rifts, and the rifts eventually become rift valleys.

paragraphs.heading: How the gap is filled
paragraphs.text: Current research indicates that complex convection in Earth's mantle lets material rise to the base of the lithosphere under each divergent boundary. This brings the area huge amounts of heat, along with a pressure drop that melts rock from the asthenosphere (the upper mantle) below the rift area. Large flood basalt or lava flows form. As the two plates move apart, the space they leave is filled with new crustal material that comes from molten magma forming below. An eruption affects only part of the boundary at any one time, but when one occurs it fills in the opening gap.

paragraphs.heading: Younger rock near the boundary
paragraphs.text: Over millions of years, tectonic plates may travel many hundreds of kilometers away from the two sides of a divergent boundary. Because of this, the rocks nearest a boundary are younger than rocks farther off on the same plate.

paragraphs.heading: Where to find them
paragraphs.text: In oceanic lithosphere, the typical divergent boundaries are the rifts of the oceanic ridge system, which includes the East Pacific Rise and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. In continental lithosphere, they are rift valleys such as the East African Great Rift Valley. New divergent boundaries that start at triple junctions are sometimes thought to be linked to hotspots. At a hotspot, exceedingly large convective cells carry very large quantities of hot material from the asthenosphere close to the surface. The kinetic energy is thought to be enough to break the lithosphere apart.

paragraphs.heading: Faults across the ridge
paragraphs.text: At divergent boundaries, massive fault zones can form in the oceanic ridge system. Spreading is generally not uniform. Where neighbouring blocks of ridge spread at different rates, massive transform faults occur. These are the fracture zones, many of which have names, and they are a major source of earthquakes under the sea. A map of the seafloor shows a pattern of blocky structures, separated by linear features that run perpendicular to the ridge axis.

paragraphs.heading: The magnetic stripes
paragraphs.text: Mid-ocean ridges gave one of the key pieces of evidence that forced acceptance of the seafloor spreading hypothesis. Airborne geomagnetic surveys showed a strange pattern: magnetic reversals arranged symmetrically on the two sides of ridge centers. It was much too regular to be a coincidence, because the widths of the opposing bands matched too closely. Scientists had been studying polar reversals, and Lawrence Morley, Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews made the link: the magnetic banding corresponds directly to Earth's polar reversals. Measuring the ages of the rocks in each band confirmed this. The banding gives a map of both spreading rate and polar reversals across time and space.
